Risk Management Status

Executive Summary
Illinois Basin – Decatur Project (IBDP) is a project undertaken by the Midwest Geological Sequestration
       Consortium (MGSC), whose members include Illinois State Geologic Survey (ISGS), Archer Daniels
       Midland Corporation (ADM), Schlumberger Carbon Services, and others. It is a “Phase III large-scale
       demonstration project” of the Regional Carbon Sequestration Program funded by National Energy
       Technology Laboratory, U.S. Department of Energy. Risk management for IBDP began with project
        kickoff in 2008, continues presently, and will carry on for the duration of the project. Through December
       2011, the stages of risk management emphasized risk identification, evaluation, treatment development,
      and treatment execution tracking; near-term future emphasis is placed on risk re-evaluation in light of
        early monitoring data to be acquired in mid-2012.

During two workshops held in early 2008, more than 40 professionals most knowledgeable in project facts,
        uncertainties, and plans evaluated 123 concepts called “FEPs” – Features, Events, and Processes – for
        their associated risks to project goals and values. The defined values include safety, research objectives,
      and public acceptance as well as technical aspects of successfully storing and monitoring injected CO2.
        In six working groups, the experts quantified Severity and Likelihood of negative impact (whose
        product, S*L, is defined as “Risk”) according to five-point categorical scales. Evaluations were made by
       both group consensus and independent scoring; the independent scores prevented the potential
       obscuration of valid “worst-case” concepts that could occur through averaging of group scores or
       through group dynamics.

The higher-risk FEPs (roughly the top half of the evaluated list) were used to develop approximately 100
       concrete scenarios that would result – if they occurred – in negative impact. The scenarios were used in
       turn to develop >200 risk treatments (risk response actions / “RRAs”) involving well engineering,
       subsurface characterization, computer modeling, monitoring, public communications, and other efforts.
       Risk treatments are actions that reduce the severity and/or the likelihood of negative impact.

Risk treatments were grouped into 29 areas of function or expertise, called Risk Response Action Groups
       (RRAGs). Each RRAG was assigned to a specific individual responsible for organizing and documenting
       the completion of the actions. Documentation was maintained on an electronic spreadsheet developed
      by the risk manager and accessible 24/7 to all individuals involved in risk treatments.

Early in the project, half of the 206 RRAs were identified as “required to be completed before injection start”,
        unless their incomplete status were deemed acceptable by the IBDP Principal Investigator (PI). When
       the injection permit was received from Illinois EPA, about 25 of those actions were not documented as
       complete. Their status was reviewed by the Schlumberger Carbon Services Risk Manager and Project
       Manager, and the IBDP PI. Before authorizing compressor start, the Schlumberger Carbon Services PM
      and IBDP PI agreed that the outstanding items did not pose immediate threats to safety, were
       adequately mitigated through other actions, or were no longer pertinent; and that accordingly overall
        risk stood at an acceptable level. The considerable development of knowledge about the project’s
       subsurface details, engineered systems, and human systems, during the two years after the RRA list was
        generated, established confidence that risk levels were acceptably low.

INTRODUCTION
Illinois Basin – Decatur Project (IBDP) is a project undertaken by the Midwest Geological Sequestration
       Consortium (MGSC). MGSC members include Illinois State Geologic Survey (ISGS), Archer Daniels
       Midland Corporation (ADM), Schlumberger Carbon Services, Trimeric Corporation, State geological
       surveys in Kentucky and Indiana, and academic and research institutions across the United States. IBDP
          is a “Phase III large-scale demonstration project” of the Regional Carbon Sequestration Program funded
      by National Energy Technology Laboratory, U.S. Department of Energy. The central purpose of IBDP is to
        safely inject, into a suitable subsurface geologic reservoir, one million tons of carbon dioxide (CO2) over
       a period of three years, and to monitor its fate and transport during this period and subsequent years.

Risk management for IBDP began with the project kickoff meeting in 2008, continues now, and will carry on for
       the duration of the project. Through December 2011, the stages of risk management emphasized risk
        identification and evaluation; developing risk treatments (risk response actions); executing and tracking
        risk treatments. In early to mid-2012 (i.e. at the time this report is written), risk management emphasis
          is placed on risk re-evaluation in light of (1) Early monitoring data being acquired in mid-2012; and (2)
       Operational experience.

Detailed descriptions of risk assessment processes and early results are given in the two papers listed below.
       Copies of both papers may be obtained online, or from ISGS or Schlumberger Carbon Services. These risk
       assessment processes have been described in several semi-public meetings, chiefly under the auspices
        of International Energy Agency, Greenhouse Gas Program (IEAGHG), but in other semi-public forums as
        well.

RISK WORKSHOPS
During two workshops held in February and March 2008, more than 40 professionals most knowledgeable in
        project facts, uncertainties, and plans evaluated 123 concepts called “FEPs” – Features, Events, and
       Processes – for their associated risks to project goals and values. A list of 178 FEPs pertinent to CO2
       Capture and Sequestration (CCS) projects has been developed by Quintessa Ltd. and published by
      IEAGHG; the FEPs list used for IBDP was a slightly refined version of the Quintessa list. FEPs are
        relatively broad concepts; their evaluation does not require identifying specific chains of events
        (scenarios).

To evaluate risk, it is mandatory to define the specific entities or values that may be at risk. For IBDP, the defined
        project values include safety, research objectives, and public acceptance, in addition to technical aspects
        of successfully storing and monitoring injected CO2.

Organized into six topical working groups (three of which met at each of the two workshops) (Appendix A), the
       experts quantified Severity and Likelihood of negative impact according to five-point categorical scales.

The product of Severity and Likelihood, S*L, is defined as “Risk”, and the quantified magnitude of “risk”
       can therefore vary along a scale from 1 to 25. This calculated “risk” value is the main comparator or
       ranking value of the evaluated entities.

Evaluations were made both by group consensus and by follow-up independent scoring. Generally, averaged
       group scores produce the most consistent ranking of risked entities. Nonetheless, independent scoring is
        also done to counter potential “groupthink” effects, and to prevent potentially obscuring valid “worst-
        case” concepts.
RISK WORKSHOP OUTCOMES
After all FEPs were evaluated and ranked in terms of Risk = S*L, the higher-risk FEPs (roughly the top half of the
       evaluated list) were used to develop >200 concrete scenarios (Appendix B) that would result – if they
       occurred – in negative impact to one or more project values. In contrast to FEPs, scenarios are specific
      and well defined chains of events. Only scenarios that have plausibly significant impact are addressed. In
        turn, the higher-risk scenarios were used to develop >200 risk treatments (risk response actions /
       “RRAs”) that involve well engineering, subsurface characterization, computer modeling, monitoring,
        public communications, and other efforts.
RISK MANAGEMENT
The set of risk treatments was subdivided among 29 areas of function or expertise. The set of scenarios was also
       uniquely subdivided among the same 29 areas (Appendix B). Each “risk response action group” (RRAG)
          is assigned to a specific individual who is responsible for organizing and documenting the completion of
       defined risk treatments, and is also responsible more generally for managing the risk associated with a
        set of scenarios. Other individuals are “Accountable for” the defined risk treatments, or are to be
       “Consulted with” or “Informed”, as shown in a “RACI” chart (Appendix D). Documentation is maintained
      on an electronic spreadsheet developed by the risk manager and accessible 24/7 to all individuals
       involved in executing, documenting, and verifying risk treatments.

Risk treatments (Appendix C) are actions that reduce the severity and/or the likelihood of negative impact. In
       standard terminology, reductions in likelihood are referred to as “preventions”, while reductions in
        severity are called “mitigations”. For a given level of effort, preventions are normally preferred because
       they reduce risk for all risk receptors (project values), while mitigations typically reduce risk only for
         specific receptors. In general, mitigations are applied where sufficient prevention is impossible (e.g. for
        uncontrollable environmental variables such as severe weather) or impractical. Risk treatments vary in
        complexity: some are relatively simple actions that can be unambiguously determined as complete,
       while others entail developing detailed plans that either (a) Will be used during normal project
        execution, or (b) Will only be used contingently, if a specific situation occurs.
PRE-INJECTION EVALUATION
Early in the project, approximately 85 of the 200 RRAs were identified as “required for completion before
        injection start”, unless their incomplete status were to be deemed acceptable by the IBDP Principal
        Investigator (PI). As progress was made toward the start of injection, many of these actions were

completed, were documented as complete by their respective “Responsible” parties, and were verified
       as complete by their respective “Accountable” parties.

At the moment when the injection permit was received from Illinois EPA, about 25 of the defined risk treatments
       remained not documented as complete (some actions were known to have been completed, yet were not
      documented as such). Given the desire to commence injection as soon as practical, the status of actions
       not documented as complete was reviewed by the Schlumberger Carbon Services Risk Manager and
        Project Manager and the IBDP PI. The Schlumberger Carbon Services PM and IBDP PI agreed that the
        risks addressed by the outstanding response actions did not pose immediate threats to safety and/or
      were adequately addressed through other actions. Consequently, the IBDP PI determined that residual
        risk stood at an overall acceptable level, and authorized compressor start. The considerable
       development of knowledge about the project’s subsurface details, engineered systems, and human
       systems, during the two years after the RRA list was generated, established confidence that risk levels
      were acceptably low.
MID-PROJECT RISK RE-EVALUATION
By mid-2012, significant operational experience will have been gained, and significant additional project data
         will be available. The new data will consist of several rounds of sampling from the in-reservoir
       observation well, continuous pressure and temperature data at multiple surface points and depth levels,
      and processed 3D seismic data from which CO2 plume distribution will be interpreted. All of this
       information will form the basis for re-evaluating risk at a greater level of knowledge than existed at
        project start.

In general terms, the objectives of mid-project re-evaluation are the same as those in the early-project
        evaluation: to identify and evaluate sources of risk, to plan actions that will reduce those risks that are
       unacceptably high, and to initiate a management structure that will maintain risk at acceptable levels
      and will document that this is the case. The key difference from the initial evaluation is the evolution of
       the project from the initiation-creation stage toward a progressive development phase, with an eye
       toward beginning the establishment and documentation of the conditions that will eventually enable
        project closure. While the overall project values will remain the same, the evolution of project activities
      and shorter-term objectives may call for revisiting the scales of potential negative impact.
